title: Nvidia launches Minerva, an AIOps platform for GPU-cluster failure detection
subtitle: Unveiled at GTC Berlin, Minerva fuses telemetry from GPUs, networks, storage, and schedulers into a single data-center map and uses ML to flag likely-failing components.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Nvidia introduced Minerva at GTC Berlin on October 22. It is an AIOps platform aimed at the operators of very large GPU clusters, combining telemetry from GPUs, SuperNICs, switches, storage, job schedulers, and the models themselves into a single dynamic knowledge graph of the data center. It then uses machine learning to learn normal behavior, predict failures, and group related alerts into one incident with a probable cause. A native AI assistant answers natural-language queries about the cluster.

The metric Nvidia leads with is 'goodput' — not raw GPU hours but hours of useful training work actually delivered. The reason that matters: at hundreds of thousands of GPUs, a single failing optical cable or thermally throttled rack can quietly degrade throughput for a whole run. Minerva's pitch is that an entire training job's effective speed depends on the slowest healthy component, and that finding it fast is now a product in its own right.

Named adopters include IREN, which is already using Minerva; Bitdeer AI, IBM, Jio, Lambda, and Tesla, which plan to adopt it; and Dell, Lenovo, and Supermicro, which will resell it to their own customers. Pricing was not disclosed. The product fits a broader move by Nvidia from selling silicon to selling the operational stack that makes the silicon productive — observability, orchestration, networking — which is how a chip vendor becomes a platform vendor.

A note for learners: 'AI factory' is marketing, but 'goodput' is engineering. If you are learning distributed systems, the useful lesson here is that at scale, the hard problem is not training a model once — it is keeping tens of thousands of components correlated, healthy, and useful for weeks on end. The tooling that solves that quietly tends to matter more than the next benchmark.
